Our past magic systems have been, in a word, a clusterfuck. In all honestly, Ki and Corgi are both OP and/or broken as fuck (and no others have mattered). Here's my proposal for a new, nonbroken, versatile system based off DnD magic. Or, you know, related to.

* Each mortal (read: non-godly) living entity has an internal reservoir of magic. * This magic, though generally a bit hand-wavy, can be projected from the internal reservoir in the form of spells. These spells can take the form of anything from simple cantrips to tornadoes depending on the amount of magic expended and the proficiency of the caster. * The scale of spells scales with the proficiency of a caster. A master could move molecules or cliff faces, while a apprentice could only do midrange things with no large of finesse. With proficiency also comes efficiency in casting. * Enchantments can be made, alchemy, potions, your typical high magic system. * Multiple casters can fuel a single spell to increase the proficiency and mana pool. * At the start of the game only base elemental magics exist, though new branches can be opened up by godly or mortal means, such as psykomancy. * Overexertion in casting can result in: heart attacks, aneurysm, spontaneous combustion, nuclear fission, vacuum metastability event
A Proposal for a Unified Magic System in the New Season
No nuclear fission. I'm not giving you the excuse to set off nukes no matter what. I can have other contentions, but I'm too tired to think of them right now.
It's only nukes with uranium or plutonium. Anything lighter and it just turns into a mound of gibs.
Without a more fleshed-out idea, I'm going to have to say NO

I don't see how this would solve anything. Both Ki and Corgi would be examples of this system with only superficial modifications.

This system looks more to me like a description of the traditional magic system, rather than a look at what worked and what didn't in this season.

What didn't work:

Ki and Corgi. Both were "control mana using caster's skill/magitek for arbitrary results" with some guidelines on what was easy or hard (which were mostly ignored).

What Did:

Umbralochian magic was forgotten about later on but did find some use among schrykes/med'ja. Necromancy got used but I don't think that arc was ever resolved.

Necromancy was really just "pray to god of death for stuff" so I don't think it really counts as a magic system.

Umbralochian magic was more interesting. Practitioners were restricted to one type of thing, and there was a tangible cost to its use that scaled well with the act performed. It was completely open-ended, but the cost for OP actions was prohibitive.

Ki and Corgi magics failed because the only restrictions on their use was user skill level, which can easily be handwaved. Umbralochian magic avoided abuse despite being basically omnipotence in an area by being expensive. This is what I think is the key to having open-ended magic systems.

Better that coming up with a set of rules that heavily restricts the form magic can take without really solving any problems, I think it would be better to just provide this guideline:

Power has a price.

That's it. If using magic has a drawback of some sort its harder to abuse (assuming the magic and drawback are reasonably balanced and designed, of course, if the drawback is that you itch and the power is to instantly kill anyone its clearly imbalanced for instance).

That's for open-ended magic systems, ones where the scope is heavily restricted wouldn't necessarily need drawbacks (though they would still be a good idea).
